title: Skooland: Multi-Tenant School Operating System
excerpt: Skooland runs a school's daily operations from one platform. Each school gets a public website and separate portals for students, staff, parents, and management. It covers attendance, CBT exams, broadsheets and report cards, fees, timetables, and admissions, and it syncs with the Queez CBT offline exam server.
problem: Many schools keep attendance, results, fees, and admissions in separate spreadsheets, paper files, and one-off tools. Their websites are often old and disconnected from everything else. Schools that run exams offline have no clean way to get those results into their records.
goal: Build one platform where a school signs up, gets its own website and portals, and runs attendance, exams, results, and fees in one place, with each school's data kept separate.
architecture: A Next.js frontend serves the marketing site, the school admin console, each school's public website, and the four portals. Middleware maps subdomains to the right school and portal. A NestJS backend serves the portal APIs and stores each school's data in its own PostgreSQL schema. A separate Prisma database holds accounts, subscriptions, and website content. Socket.io pushes live exam monitoring to management.
challenges: Keeping school data isolated while sharing one codebase and one database server. Changing the database layout for schools that already exist. Letting an offline exam server talk to the platform without sharing a school's admin login.
solutions: Gave each school its own PostgreSQL schema, with slugs sanitized before they reach any query, and created schemas on demand with idempotent DDL. Added column-level ALTER statements so existing schools pick up new fields. Built scoped API keys for the offline sync: up to five per school, stored as SHA-256 hashes, shown only once, and rotatable at any time.
tradeOffs: A schema per school gives strong isolation and makes it easy to export or remove one school's data. The cost is that every database change has to run on every school's schema, not just once.
lessons: CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS does not change tables that already exist. Existing schools hit missing-column errors until I added explicit migrations that run on every school's schema.
outcome: A working multi-tenant platform with a school admin console, four role-based portals, a website editor for each school, and a documented sync API that connects it to the Queez CBT offline exam suite.

title: Chiko AI: Research Assistant with Citations & Bias Check
excerpt: Chiko AI is a Chrome extension and web app that reads the page you are on and gives you the key points, possible biases, open questions, and numbers it found. Every point links to the sentence it came from. Saved pages can be grouped into research projects and questioned together.
problem: Chatbot summaries sound sure of themselves, but you can't check them. A plain summary also only repeats the page. It doesn't tell you what the page leaves out or where it might be biased.
goal: Build a reading tool that keeps the page next to the summary, links every claim to its source sentence, and points out bias and unanswered questions.
architecture: A Manifest V3 extension pulls the page text inside the user's browser and shows results in the Chrome side panel. A FastAPI backend runs the analysis, stores the library in PostgreSQL, and uses Redis for jobs and rate limits. A Next.js site holds the marketing pages, the waitlist, and the dashboard, including the research workspace.
challenges: Getting a click on a citation to find and highlight the right sentence on pages with messy HTML. Letting people use their own AI keys without keeping those keys in the browser. Asking Chrome for as little page access as possible.
solutions: Anchored each citation to the source text and added a content script that scrolls to the match and highlights it. Stored bring-your-own keys encrypted on the server and deleted the old local copies. Kept host permissions limited to Chiko's own services.
tradeOffs: Reading the page in the browser means it works behind logins and paywalls, but it also means the extension needs a content script that runs on arbitrary sites. That is the main thing Chrome's review looks at.
lessons: What you promise in the privacy policy and permission forms has to match the code. I found and fixed two places where it didn't before submitting.
outcome: A working extension, website, dashboard, and backend, now in pre-launch with a public waitlist at waitlist.chikoai.com ahead of the Chrome Web Store release.

title: UNIFIVE: Browser Pixel Game Studio
excerpt: UNIFIVE lets you make 2D pixel games in the browser with nothing to install. It has side-scrolling and top-down scene editors, visual block programming, a sprite animation timeline, single-file project export, and play testing on mobile.
problem: Beginner game engines often need a multi-gigabyte install, an account, or a build step before you can make anything. Browser-based ones tend to lock your project into their platform, and few support both platformer and top-down games.
goal: Make a game editor that runs in any modern browser with no build step, no install, and no backend, and that handles both platformer and top-down games.
architecture: A static HTML and JavaScript app runs a p5.js canvas inside a split layout for the scene, the block logic, and sprite properties. Separate modules handle rendering, running the block code, audio, and saving projects. A Web Worker compresses project files with gzip in the background.
challenges: Running a scene editor, a visual code interpreter, and sprite animation all in the browser without freezing the main thread.
solutions: Kept separate state for platformer and top-down modes, grouped canvas draws into one render loop, used the built-in Compression Streams API for exports, and limited how many steps the block interpreter runs per frame so a long loop can't hang the page.
tradeOffs: Everything runs on the user's machine, so there is no hosting cost and no data leaves the browser. Scenes with a lot of entities depend on how fast the user's hardware is.
lessons: Creative tools stay smooth when rendering, scripting, and asset loading are kept apart and talk through typed events.
outcome: A browser editor where students and developers can design, animate, test, and share a full pixel game as one compressed file.

title: Queez CBT: Offline Examination Suite
excerpt: Queez CBT runs computer-based exams without internet, for schools and testing centers. Three apps talk over local Wi-Fi: a host server (Express and SQLite), an Assessment Manager for writing tests, and a locked-down Student Portal for desktop and Android.
problem: Web exam portals stop working when the internet drops in a school computer lab. Schools also worry about students switching screens, slow marking by hand, and network setup in places with no IT staff.
goal: Build an exam system that handles math-heavy questions with KaTeX, locks the student's screen during the test, and keeps a live session in sync over local Wi-Fi with no internet.
architecture: Three apps: a server that hosts the exam, an Assessment Manager for staff, and a hardened Student Portal. They find each other on the local network with UDP broadcasts, then use REST and WebSockets. Exam records are written to an embedded SQLite database.
challenges: Keeping a student's answers when the Wi-Fi drops, stopping students from tampering with the exam window, and rendering dense math notation without lag.
solutions: Added automatic discovery with UDP beacons, native kiosk-mode lockdown, an answer queue in IndexedDB that can safely retry, and a different shuffle of questions and options for each candidate.
tradeOffs: Windows installers and Android APKs are more work to ship than one website. In return, exams keep running through power or internet outages.
lessons: When you can't trust the network, you need local storage fallbacks, queues that behave the same on every retry, and heartbeats over the local network.
outcome: Used in schools for timed exams, with live hall monitoring, instant scoring, printable candidate slips, and branded PDF score reports.

title: Anonfly: Private Real-Time Messaging Platform
excerpt: Anonfly is an anonymous, end-to-end encrypted chat platform made of an API service, a React web client, and an SDK monorepo. It has disposable identities, real-time messages over WebSockets and SSE, Redis pub/sub routing, and packages for React, Next.js, and the command line.
problem: Most chat tools ask for a phone number or email, which leaves a trail of metadata. Developers who want anonymous messaging in their own apps also have no ready-made SDK for modern JavaScript frameworks.
goal: Ship Anonfly both as a chat app people can use and as an open-source SDK, with anonymous identities, encrypted messages, and packages that are easy to integrate.
architecture: The backend handles session authorization, room presence, Redis pub/sub channels, and storing encrypted messages. The browser client holds the cryptographic keys and shows the live chat. A Turborepo monorepo publishes the core, React, Next.js, and CLI libraries.
challenges: Keeping message latency under 50ms across many active rooms, protecting disposable tokens, and versioning several packages in one monorepo cleanly.
solutions: Used Redis pub/sub to pass messages between WebSocket server instances, checked cryptographic signatures on every incoming socket, and used Turborepo with Changesets to release each library on its own.
tradeOffs: Splitting the project into a backend, a client, and several packages means more build setup. It also means other developers can embed Anonfly in their own apps.
lessons: Security-focused code is easier to maintain when the crypto, the transport, and the UI live in separate packages.
outcome: A complete encrypted chat platform with disposable room codes, message delivery under 50ms, and published SDK packages for frontend and Node.js.

title: WorkUp Cards: Business Card Generator
excerpt: WorkUp Cards is a business card designer that runs in the browser. You pick a template, edit the front and back live, check the layout, and download a print-ready PNG, all without a server.
problem: Freelancers and small business owners who need a card quickly usually end up buying a design suite or using a server-side tool that is slow and sends their details to someone else's server.
goal: Build a fast card maker in the browser with editable templates, instant live preview, and a high-resolution export ready for printing.
architecture: A React app where the form fields drive an SVG and HTML card layout. Zod validates the form, and a canvas exporter turns the card into a high-resolution image in the browser.
challenges: Getting custom fonts and vector layouts onto a canvas without clipped text or blur on high-DPI screens.
solutions: Set the card size with print-based CSS dimensions, debounced the re-render while typing, and scaled the html2canvas capture by the device pixel ratio so exports stay sharp.
tradeOffs: Exporting in the browser means no server costs. Older phones can run low on memory when rendering a large image.
lessons: A live editor feels instant when updating form state and capturing the canvas are separate steps, and the capture is debounced.
outcome: A client-side card generator with several templates, a responsive preview, and one-click PNG downloads.

title: WorldTimeSage: Global Timezone Dashboard
excerpt: WorldTimeSage is a timezone dashboard and reference tool. It has searchable world clocks, country timezone details, offset comparisons, and works offline as an installable PWA.
problem: People who work with teams in other countries need more than a clock app. They want to look up a country quickly, see daylight saving changes, and still use the tool when they're traveling without internet.
goal: Build a timezone dashboard with search, offset comparison between regions, pinned locations, and full offline use as an installable PWA.
architecture: A React single-page app with Redux Toolkit. It is split into dashboard, country details, offline cache, and settings views, and a service worker caches the location data.
challenges: Getting local time offsets and daylight saving right across very different regions while keeping the interface light and fast.
solutions: Used the browser's built-in Intl.DateTimeFormat instead of a date library to keep the bundle small, indexed the location data for instant search, and set up service worker caching for offline use.
tradeOffs: Shipping detailed location data makes the first cache larger, but every lookup keeps working with no connection.
lessons: For a PWA like this, try the browser's own APIs, such as Intl, before adding a heavy date library.
outcome: An installable timezone dashboard with country search that returns in under a second, side-by-side clocks for multiple cities, and offline support.

title: AsterMail: Dynamic Email Delivery API
excerpt: AsterMail is a small backend that sends transactional emails using SMTP credentials supplied with each request. It validates input, rate limits, logs requests, caches in memory, and returns structured errors.
problem: Developers building small apps often want to send a few transactional emails without paying for an enterprise email service or hardcoding SMTP credentials into their main repo.
goal: Build a REST API that validates an email request, sets up the SMTP connection from the request's own credentials, and returns the same response format every time.
architecture: An Express 5 service with input validation middleware, a Nodemailer transport created per request, Helmet security headers, and an LRU cache to avoid setting up the same transport repeatedly.
challenges: Stopping abuse while keeping delivery fast, and reporting clear errors when an outside mail server rejects the credentials.
solutions: Validated every payload with Express Validator, added rate limiting by IP, used one error format for all failures, and kept transport connections in an LRU cache.
tradeOffs: Accepting credentials per request gives client apps full control over their mail server. It also means the input has to be sanitized carefully to prevent email header injection.
lessons: A small service stays reliable when logging, connection reuse, and security middleware are set up once at the router level.
outcome: A live email service that sends over each caller's SMTP server, validates input automatically, and returns structured errors.

title: Geemex: Gaming Landing Page Template
excerpt: Geemex is a landing page template for gaming communities and game titles, built with Vue 3 and Vite. It has a character carousel, responsive pricing tiers, an FAQ accordion, and call-to-action banners aimed at indie games and gaming brands.
problem: Indie studios and tournament organizers rarely have time to build a custom marketing page, and generic templates don't have the high-contrast look that gaming needs.
goal: Make a gaming landing page template that looks like a game, loads quickly, and is built from clean, reusable components.
architecture: A Vue 3 single-page app on Vite 6 and Tailwind CSS 4. Each section, such as the hero, character spotlights, pricing, FAQ, and download links, is its own single-file component.
challenges: Getting a high-contrast, animated look without layout shifts or slow loads on mobile.
solutions: Used light CSS transitions for card and character hover states, let Vite's build pipeline optimize the assets, and typed every component prop in TypeScript.
tradeOffs: A static page is fast and easy to maintain. Tournament sign-ups would need a backend API added later.
lessons: A template gets reused when its typography, layout, and component slots make it quick to change the branding.
outcome: A small, production-ready gaming template with Vue 3 components that loads fast and adapts to any screen size.

title: Asterixh School: Educational Portal & Admissions Hub
excerpt: Asterixh School is a school website and online admissions portal built with Next.js 16 (App Router) and TypeScript. It covers academics, events and notices, admission requirements, and inquiry forms across several pages.
problem: Parents and students often can't find admission dates, fees, or curriculum details on old school websites, which also look bad on a phone.
goal: Build a modern school site that explains the school's approach, makes it easy to send an admissions inquiry, and works well on phones and desktops.
architecture: Next.js App Router renders the academics, admissions, faculty, and news pages on the server. The enrollment and contact forms validate on the client. The header, navigation, and footer are shared across pages.
challenges: Fitting a lot of information across several grade levels onto pages that stay clear and quick to move between.
solutions: Organized the site around clear navigation categories with breadcrumbs, used card grids for curriculum highlights, and validated the application forms with Zod.
tradeOffs: File-based routing makes pages load quickly. A feature like looking up a student's grades would need an admin backend.
lessons: On a school site, the main actions, like sending an admission inquiry or checking term dates, should be within two clicks of the homepage.
outcome: A mobile-friendly school site with fast pages, clear admission steps, and organized academic information for families.

title: SMS: School Management System
excerpt: SMS is a full-stack school management platform with a separate frontend and backend. It covers role-based access, attendance, student profiles, conduct records, and fee workflows, on Express, PostgreSQL, and Supabase.
problem: School administrators often keep student records, attendance, fees, and staff duties in separate spreadsheets and paper files. That leads to mistakes and slow audits.
goal: Build one system where administrators, teachers, and bursars work in the same platform, each with strict limits on what they can see and do.
architecture: The frontend uses React Router, React Query, and Zustand to cache state across the admin screens. The backend is a set of Express services for authentication, student rosters, attendance, conduct records, and fee receipts, writing to PostgreSQL on Supabase.
challenges: Enforcing fine-grained permissions across many screens while keeping the frontend routes in step with the backend's authorization checks.
solutions: Added role-based route guards on the client, checked tokens and role claims on every API route, and tuned the database queries with foreign keys and indexes.
tradeOffs: Keeping the frontend and backend in separate repositories means the API contract has to be kept in sync. It also lets each side scale and deploy on its own.
lessons: Permissions hold up better when they are rules in the database, not just conditions in the UI.
outcome: A school operations system that handles student enrolment, daily attendance, fee verification, and role-based staff administration.

title: motion-lyte.js: Declarative Web Animation Library
excerpt: motion-lyte.js is a small animation library that works with any framework and is driven by HTML data attributes. It supports scroll, hover, and toggle triggers, comes with a React hook and a Vite plugin, and adds no extra runtime for basic effects.
problem: A lot of animation libraries ship a large runtime or need imperative setup code that clutters your templates and slows the first load.
goal: Make a small animation tool where you add motion by writing HTML data attributes, with React and Vite support for people who want it.
architecture: A small runtime scans the page for elements with data-motion attributes and uses Intersection Observer for scroll triggers. It ships a core engine, TypeScript definitions, a React hook, and a Vite plugin, bundled with tsup.
challenges: Designing attribute syntax that is easy to read while still supporting staggered delays, custom easing curves, and scroll thresholds.
solutions: Built an internal registry that maps each attribute to a hardware-accelerated CSS transform, and shared Intersection Observers across elements to avoid layout thrashing.
tradeOffs: Data attributes make it quick to adopt and keep it small. Complex multi-step timelines are still easier in an imperative library like GSAP.
lessons: Developer tools get used when they work in plain HTML with no setup and also come with typed wrappers for React and Vite.
outcome: An open-source animation library with a runtime under 4KB, Vitest tests, and drop-in use on static and React sites.

title: Catalyst Consultant: Business Consulting Landing Page
excerpt: Catalyst Consultant is a landing page for a business advisory firm, built to turn visitors into booked consultations. It is a static Vite site with custom CSS and motion-lyte.js, and covers services, consultant profiles, client testimonials, pricing, and a booking form.
problem: Consulting firms need to look credible and turn visitors into bookings, and slow, bloated theme templates work against that.
goal: Build a fast one-page consulting site with a clear copy structure and small touches of motion, to get more people to book.
architecture: A static Vite build that serves pre-rendered HTML and optimized CSS. motion-lyte.js handles the scroll reveals and hover effects on the cards, testimonials, and booking form.
challenges: Keeping the page looking premium, with accordions and carousels, while keeping its weight low and the first paint under one second.
solutions: Gave each section a clear visual hierarchy, added motion attributes only to key headlines and statistics, and built a responsive appointment form.
tradeOffs: A static site loads fast and has little to attack. Real scheduling needs a calendar or webhook service added.
lessons: Landing pages convert better when the main promise is above the fold and backed up by testimonials, clear pricing, and a simple call to action.
outcome: A responsive consulting page that loads in under a second and doubles as a demo of motion-lyte.js.

title: Resin Art: Creative Portfolio & Product Catalog
excerpt: Resin Art is a portfolio and inquiry storefront for handmade resin crafts, built with Next.js 16 and TypeScript. It pairs large photo galleries and a product catalog with email inquiries and a direct WhatsApp order link.
problem: A maker selling handmade pieces needs more than a photo gallery. They need a catalog with details, a way to build trust, and a direct way to quote custom orders without paying an e-commerce platform's fees.
goal: Build a good-looking portfolio and catalog that shows the resin pieces and sends interested buyers straight to WhatsApp or email.
architecture: Next.js App Router handles the layout and catalog pages. JSON files hold the product details and testimonials, and API routes validate custom order inquiries with Zod and send them through Nodemailer.
challenges: Showing high-resolution product photos without slow mobile loads, and making the jump to WhatsApp for a custom quote easy on a phone.
solutions: Used Next.js image optimization with WebP, added category filters, and built click-to-chat WhatsApp links that already include the product name.
tradeOffs: A catalog with inquiries suits custom, one-off pieces. Selling standard items in volume would eventually need a proper payment checkout.
lessons: For handmade and custom goods, a conversation on WhatsApp tends to convert better than a multi-step cart.
outcome: A mobile-first brand portfolio and catalog that brings in custom order inquiries through email and WhatsApp.
